## Inversion

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition (Inversion).**
Given a circle $\omega$ with center $O$ and radius $r$, if a point $X^\star$ lies on the ray $OX$ and satisfies $OX\cdot OX^\star =r^2$, then $X^\star$ is called the **inverse** of $X$ with respect to $\omega$. When there is no ambiguity about the inversion, $X^\star$ denotes the inverse of $X$ unless otherwise stated.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The inverse of $O$ with respect to $\omega$ is the **point at infinity** $P_{\infty}$.
:::

::: {#cor-4point1}
$(A^\star )^\star =A$.
:::

::: {#lem-4point1}
If $O$ is the center of inversion, then $\triangle OAB\stackrel{-}{\sim}\triangle OB^\star A^\star$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By power of a point at $O$, $A,B,A^\star ,B^\star$ are concyclic, from which the opposite similarity follows immediately.
:::

::: {#cor-4point2}
Any line passing through the center of inversion is mapped to itself under inversion.
:::

::: {#lem-4point2}
The inverse of a circle $\Omega$ (with center $X$) passing through the center of inversion $O$ is a line not passing through $O$ that is perpendicular to $OX$, and vice versa.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Consider the antipode $D$ of $O$ on $\Omega$. For any point $P\neq O$ on $\Omega$, we have
$$\measuredangle OD^\star P^\star =\measuredangle DPO=90^\circ.$$
:::

::: {#lem-4point3}
The inverse of a circle $\Omega$ not passing through the center of inversion $O$ is another circle not passing through $O$, and the line joining the centers of the two circles passes through $O$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $AB$ be the diameter of $\Omega$ whose line passes through $O$. For any point $P$ on $(AB)$, we have
$$\measuredangle A^\star P^\star B^\star =\measuredangle P^\star A^\star O+\measuredangle OB^\star P^\star =\measuredangle OPA+\measuredangle BPO=90^\circ.$$
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
A **generalized circle** is a circle determined by three points; if one of the points is $P_{\infty}$, the generalized circle is the line passing through the other two points.
:::

::: {#cor-4point3}
The inverse of a generalized circle is also a generalized circle.
:::

::: {#thm-4point1}
Inversion is conformal; that is, it preserves the angles between intersecting curves.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Considering the tangent lines at the point of intersection, inversion maps them to two circles passing through the center of inversion, and angle chasing shows that their angle of intersection is preserved.
:::

::: {#lem-4point4}
The inverse of the circumcenter of $(OAB)$ is the reflection of $O$ across $A^\star B^\star$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By perpendicularity, the inverse of the antipode of $O$ on $(OAB)$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to $A^\star B^\star$. Applying a homothety centered at $O$ with ratio $2$ gives the result.
:::

::: {#lem-4point5}
In a complete quadrilateral, the circumcenters of the four triangles and the Miquel point lie on a single circle.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Inverting about the Miquel point maps the four circumcenters to the reflections of the Miquel point across the four lines of the inverted configuration, which lie on the Steiner line of another complete quadrilateral. Hence the original five points are concyclic.
:::

::: {#thm-4point2}
Given points $A,B$ and an inversion circle centered at $O$ with radius $R$, we have
$$A^\star B^\star =\frac{R^2}{OA\cdot OB}\cdot AB.$$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This follows immediately from @lem-4point1.
:::

::: {#thm-4point3}
## Ptolemy's Theorem
If $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral, then
$$AB\cdot CD+AD\cdot CB=AC\cdot BD.$$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Invert about $A$. By @lem-4point2, $C^\star$ lies on the segment $B^\star D^\star$.

Thus $B^\star C^\star +C^\star D^\star =B^\star D^\star $, and applying @thm-4point2 to compute the lengths yields the identity.
:::

::: {#thm-4point4}
Given $c>0$ ($c\neq 1$) and distinct points $X,Y$, the locus of points $P$ satisfying $PX/PY=c$ is a circle.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Pick one point $Q$ satisfying the condition, so $PX\cdot QY=PY\cdot QX$.

Inverting about $Q$ gives $P^\star X^\star =P^\star Y^\star $, so the locus of $P^\star$ is the perpendicular bisector of $X^\star Y^\star $, and hence the locus of $P$ is a circle.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The circle in @thm-4point4 is called an **Apollonius circle**. The locus of points $P$ satisfying $PB/PC=AB/AC$ is called the **$A$-Apollonius circle**.
:::

::: {#lem-4point6}
If $P$ lies on the $A$-Apollonius circle, then $\measuredangle APB+\measuredangle APC=\measuredangle ABC+\measuredangle ACB$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By @thm-4point4, inverting about $A$ gives $P^\star B^\star =P^\star C^\star$.

Therefore,
$$0=\measuredangle P^\star B^\star C^\star +\measuredangle P^\star C^\star B^\star =\measuredangle P^\star B^\star A+\measuredangle AB^\star C^\star +\measuredangle P^\star C^\star A+\measuredangle AC^\star B^\star .$$
By @lem-4point1, this translates to $\measuredangle APB+\measuredangle APC=\measuredangle ABC+\measuredangle ACB$.
:::

::: {#lem-4point7}
The center of the $A$-Apollonius circle is the intersection of the tangent to $(ABC)$ at $A$ with $BC$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By the Angle Bisector Theorem, the $A$-Apollonius circle passes through the intersections of the internal and external angle bisectors of $\angle BAC$ with $BC$.

Since these two points form a diameter of the circle, angle chasing identifies its midpoint as the intersection of the tangent at $A$ with $BC$.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
A point $P$ inside $(ABC)$ satisfying $PA\cdot BC=PB\cdot CA=PC\cdot AB$ is called the **first isodynamic point** $X(15)$.
:::

::: {#cor-4point4}
$X(15)$ is an intersection point of the three Apollonius circles.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition (Orthogonal Circles).**
Let two circles $\omega_1,\omega_2$ with centers $O_1,O_2$ intersect at $A$ and $B$. If $\angle O_1AO_2=90^\circ$, then $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ are said to be **orthogonal**.
:::

::: {#lem-4point8}
If $\omega$ and $\Omega$ are orthogonal, then the inverse of $\omega$ with respect to $\Omega$ is $\omega$ itself.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $\omega$ and $\Omega$ intersect at $X$ and $Y$, and let $O$ be the center of $\Omega$. Then $OX$ and $OY$ are tangent to $\omega$.

Since $X$ and $Y$ are fixed by the inversion, $\omega^\star$ still passes through $X,Y$ and remains tangent to $OX,OY$, so $\omega^\star =\omega$.
:::

::: {#lem-4point9}
The $A$-Apollonius circle is invariant under inversion with respect to $(ABC)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By @lem-4point7, the segment joining the center of the $A$-Apollonius circle to $A$ is tangent to $(ABC)$.

Hence the two circles are orthogonal, and the result follows from @lem-4point8.
:::

::: {#lem-4point10}
The three Apollonius circles intersect at two points.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By @lem-4point9, the inverse of $X(15)$ with respect to $(ABC)$ also lies on all three Apollonius circles.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The second intersection point in @lem-4point10 is called the **second isodynamic point** $X(16)$.
:::

::: {#cor-4point5}
$O,X(15),X(16)$ are collinear, and $X(16)$ lies outside $(ABC)$.
:::

::: {#cor-4point6}
Inverting $\triangle ABC$ about $A$ with radius $\sqrt{AB\cdot AC}$ followed by reflecting across the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ maps $\triangle ABC$ to itself (with $B=C^\star$ and $C=B^\star$).
:::

::: {#cor-4point7}
Under the transformation in @cor-4point6, $I^\star =I_A$, and $O^\star$ is the reflection of $A$ across $BC$.
:::

::: {#lem-4point11}
The $A$-Humpty point lies on the $A$-Apollonius circle.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Apply the $\sqrt{AB\cdot AC}$-inversion followed by reflection in @cor-4point6.

By @lem-3point8 (and @lem-3point2), the image of the $A$-Humpty point is the intersection of the tangents to $(ABC)$ at $B$ and $C$, which lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$.

As shown in the proof of @thm-4point4, the image of the $A$-Apollonius circle is this same perpendicular bisector.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The isogonal conjugate of $X(15)$ is $X(13)$ (the **first isogonic center**, or **Fermat–Torricelli point**), and the isogonal conjugate of $X(16)$ is $X(14)$ (the **second isogonic center**).
:::

::: {#lem-4point12}
Let $D$ (resp. $D'$) be the third vertex of the equilateral triangle erected outward (resp. inward) on side $BC$. Under the transformation in @cor-4point6, the image of $D$ (resp. $D'$) is $X(15)$ (resp. $X(16)$).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
The circle $\omega$ centered at $B$ with radius $BC$ maps to the $B$-Apollonius circle (as verified by computing the angle and inverse of one of the intersections of $\omega$ with $AB$). Similarly, the circle centered at $C$ with radius $BC$ maps to the $C$-Apollonius circle. Hence the image of $D$ is $X(15)$, and the inward case for $D'$ follows analogously.
:::

::: {#lem-4point13}
Let $D,E,F$ be the vertices of the equilateral triangles erected outward (or all inward) on the sides of $\triangle ABC$. Then $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$ are perspective, with perspector $X(13)$ (or $X(14)$, respectively).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By @lem-4point12, since the transformation in @cor-4point6 includes a reflection across the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$, the ray $AD$ is mapped to the isogonal conjugate of $AX(15)$. Thus the lines $AD,BE,CF$ concur at the isogonal conjugate of $X(15)$ (resp. $X(16)$), which is $X(13)$ (resp. $X(14)$).
:::

::: {#cor-4point8}
Using the notation of @lem-4point12, $X(13),B,C,D$ are concyclic, and $X(14),B,C,D'$ are concyclic.
:::

::: {#thm-4point5}
Given distinct points $X$ and $Y$, as $c>0$ varies, the resulting Apollonius circles share a common radical axis (namely, the perpendicular bisector of $XY$).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Choose a circle $\omega$ with center $O$ and radius $r_\omega$ passing through $X$ and $Y$ (as $P$ varies along $\omega$, the ratio $PX/PY$ takes all positive values). Consider $\triangle PXY$.

By @lem-4point9, $OP$ is tangent to the $P$-Apollonius circle $\Omega$.

Thus $\operatorname{Pow}_{\Omega}(O)=OP^2=r_\omega^2$, which is independent of the choice of $P$ on $\omega$.

Hence $O$ lies on the radical axis of any two $P$-Apollonius circles; since the radical axis of any pair is also perpendicular to $XY$, all such Apollonius circles share the same radical axis.
:::

::: {#lem-4point14}
The triangle formed by the inverses of the vertices of $\triangle ABC$ with respect to $P$ is directly similar to the ($\alpha$-)pedal triangle of $P$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $DEF$ be the pedal triangle of $P$. Using cyclic quadrilaterals and @lem-4point1, we have
$$
\measuredangle EDF=\measuredangle EDP+\measuredangle PDF=\measuredangle ACP+\measuredangle PBA=\measuredangle PA^\star C^\star +\measuredangle B^\star A^\star P=\measuredangle B^\star A^\star C^\star ,
$$
and similarly for the other angles (the $\alpha$-pedal case follows identically by adding $\alpha$).
:::

::: {#lem-4point15}
Inverting $\triangle ABC$ about an isodynamic point produces an equilateral triangle.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
From the proof of @thm-4point4 (or @thm-4point2), all three sides of $\triangle A^\star B^\star C^\star$ have equal length.
:::

::: {#cor-4point9}
The pedal triangle of an isodynamic point is equilateral, and the Miquel point (@lem-1point1) of any inscribed equilateral triangle is an isodynamic point.
:::

::: {#lem-4point16}
Let the tangent to $(ABC)$ at $A$ intersect $BC$ at $A_1$, and define $B_1,C_1$ analogously. Then $A_1,B_1,C_1$ are collinear, and the line through them is perpendicular to the line $OX(15)X(16)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By @lem-4point7, $A_1,B_1,C_1$ are the centers of the three Apollonius circles.

Since these three circles share the common radical axis $OX(15)X(16)$, their centers are collinear along a line perpendicular to this radical axis.
:::

::: {#lem-4point17}
Using the notation of @lem-4point16, the inverse of the $A$-Dumpty point with respect to $(ABC)$ is $A_1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $D$ lie on $(ABC)$ such that $ABDC$ is a harmonic quadrilateral.

By @cor-3point4, the intersection of the tangents to $(ABC)$ at $A$ and $D$ lies on $BC$, so this intersection is $A_1$.

Angle chasing shows that $A$ and $D$ lie on $(OA_1)$; therefore, the inverse of $A_1$ with respect to $(ABC)$ is the midpoint $M_{AD}$, which is the $A$-Dumpty point.
:::

::: {#lem-4point18}
$O,K,X(15),X(16)$ are collinear along the Brocard axis.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $T_A$ be the $A$-Dumpty point, and define $T_B,T_C$ analogously.

Inverting @cor-3point7 with respect to $(ABC)$ shows that $T_A^\star ,T_B^\star ,T_C^\star ,K^\star$ are collinear on a line perpendicular to $OK$.

By @lem-4point17, $T_A^\star =A_1$ is the intersection of the tangent to $(ABC)$ at $A$ with $BC$, and similarly for $T_B^\star$ and $T_C^\star$.

By @lem-4point16, the line $T_A^\star T_B^\star T_C^\star$ is perpendicular to $OX(15)X(16)$; hence $OK$ and $OX(15)X(16)$ coincide, so $O,K,X(15),X(16)$ are collinear.
:::
